The dust motes in the Archive of Unfinished Things did not drift downward; they hung suspended in the amber light, hesitant to land, as if waiting for the gravity of a conclusion that would never arrive. 

Arthur sat at his mahogany desk, dip pen poised over a fresh ledger. His job was simple in theory, impossible in practice: catalog the remnants of human hesitation. Every day, the pneumatic tubes behind him would shudder, hiss, and spit out brass canisters containing the newest acquisitions. 

A *clunk* echoed through the quiet room. Arthur sighed, set down his pen, and walked to the intake chute. He unscrewed the warm brass cap of the canister and tipped its contents onto his blotter. 

Out spilled a cascade of sea-glass, a half-knitted cerulean scarf with the needles still impaled through the yarn, and a small, pulsing sphere of luminescence that smelled faintly of ozone and peppermint. 

Arthur picked up the glowing sphere with a pair of velvet-tipped tongs. He held it up to his monocle. Inside the swirling mist of light, he could hear a phantom voice, tinny and distant: *“Look, all I’m saying is that if you leave now, I don’t think I’ll be here when you get back, and I really just want to tell you—”* 

The voice cut off. A classic Unsaid Goodbye. Probably spoken in a crowded train station, drowned out by the screech of brakes, or swallowed whole by sudden cowardice in the doorway of a dimly lit apartment. 

He placed the sphere into a velvet-lined box, dipped his pen into the inkwell, and wrote in the ledger: *Item 8,402,911. Unsaid Goodbye. Tone: Desperate, tinged with peppermint. Origin: Unknown, likely autumn.*

That was the nature of the Archive. The universe was a notoriously tidy place—energy could neither be created nor destroyed, after all—and it despised loose ends. When a painting was abandoned halfway through, the potential energy of the unpainted canvas had to go somewhere. When a love letter was torn up and thrown into a fire, the heat took the paper, but the *intent* drifted down through the ether and landed on Arthur’s desk.

He had been the curator here for what felt like three hundred years, though there were no clocks in the Archive. Clocks implied a progression toward an end, and ends were strictly forbidden on the premises. There was only the perpetual middle.

Arthur stood up, his knees popping in the silence, and carried the box, the scarf, and the sea-glass into the Stacks. 

The Stacks stretched out infinitely in every direction, a labyrinth of towering oak bookshelves that rose into an overcast sky of indoor clouds. Narrow cobblestone paths wound between the shelves. As Arthur walked, the shelves whispered to him.

To his left, the Symphony Section hummed a dissonant, glorious cacophony of third movements that had been abandoned when their composers died or lost their minds or simply went out for a loaf of bread and forgot the melody. To his right, the Architecture Wing groaned under the weight of phantom bridges that stopped mid-span over non-existent rivers, and blueprints for utopias that had run out of funding in the third fiscal quarter.

He slotted the scarf into Textile Regrets, row 400. He poured the sea-glass into a bin marked *Collections Started on Vacations and Immediately Forgotten Upon Returning to Work*. 

The glowing sphere, however, required a trip to the Deep Vaults. 

The Unsaid things were always the heaviest. An unpainted picture was merely sad; an unsaid word was volatile. If too many of them were stored in one place, they began to react with one another, forming a critical mass of longing that could warp the floorboards and cause the indoor clouds to rain warm, salty water.

As Arthur descended the spiral iron staircase into the Vaults, the air grew thick with the ghost-scents of a million stalled moments: cheap coffee, rain on asphalt, hospital antiseptic, old paper, lilac perfume. 

Down here, the shelves were made of lead. Thousands of spheres glowed in the dark, casting a constellation of pale blues, bruised purples, and frantic reds across Arthur’s tired face. 

*“—always loved the way you—”*
*“—sorry, I was just so afraid of—”*
*“—Wait! Don’t—”*

The whispers overlapped like the murmur of a phantom ocean. Arthur found an empty slot in Row 99, nestled between a teenage confession of guilt from 1954 and a deathbed forgiveness that had arrived two seconds too late in 1812. He gently placed the peppermint-scented sphere into its cradle.

He lingered for a moment, his fingers resting on the cold lead shelf. 

People thought of their lives as a series of things they had done. They wrote resumes and obituaries filled with accomplishments, marriages, graduations, and travels. They never realized that the true shape of a human life was defined by its negative space. They were sculpted by the jobs they didn't take, the trains they missed, the apologies they choked down, the books they stopped reading on page forty-two. Every person in the waking world was walking around as the mere fraction of who they might have been, shedding their unlived potentials like dead skin cells, leaving Arthur to sweep them up.

Sometimes, the weight of it made his chest ache. He wondered what was in the Archive that belonged to him. Before he came here—if there *was* a before—had he left a half-drunk cup of tea on a counter? Had he left someone waiting in the rain? 

He couldn't remember. The Archive had a way of smoothing over a curator’s own edges until he was all middle, too. 

From far above, echoing down the spiral staircase, came a sound. 

*Clunk.*

Another canister had arrived. Somewhere up in the sunlit world, someone had just put down a guitar they would never pick up again. Someone had just backspaced over a text message that would have changed their life, sighed, and locked their phone. 

Arthur adjusted his spectacles. He turned away from the glowing constellation of almosts, placed his hand on the iron railing, and began the long climb back up the stairs. There was always more to catalog. He reached his desk, picked up his pen, and waited for the ink to dry, knowing it never quite would.
